summary:
Orbit-Deck is an aerospace crew safety dashboard built around the Apollo 13 mission. It combines machine learning, real NASA telemetry data, and 3D thermodynamic visualization into a single web application.

The AI core is an XGBoost classifier trained on 6,000 Apollo 13 telemetry data points (NASA MSC-02680), achieving ~95% accuracy in classifying fire risk into four levels: GREEN, YELLOW, ORANGE, and RED — following NASA NPR 8715.3C safety standards.

The physics engine (FastAPI backend) computes real thermodynamic flame behavior: adiabatic flame temperature via the First Law of Thermodynamics, flame morphology using Burke-Schumann diffusion theory, Grashof number for gravity effects, and Wien's Law for spectral emission — rendering a live 3D WebGL flame that changes shape based on gravity (spherical in 0G, elongated in 1G).

The dashboard features a NASA-style 5×4 risk matrix, interactive Plotly telemetry charts with MET replay, mission phase timeline, and a full crew procedures system — all in a dark aerospace glass-cockpit interface.

Stack: Python · FastAPI · XGBoost · Three.js · Plotly · HTML/CSS/JS · Docker · GitHub
details:
What it does and how it works:

Orbit-Deck is a real-time aerospace fire risk prediction system built around the Apollo 13 mission. At its core, an XGBoost machine learning model — trained on 6,000 NASA Apollo 13 telemetry data points (MSC-02680) — classifies fire hazard levels across 13 mission phases into four risk categories: GREEN, YELLOW, ORANGE, and RED, following NASA NPR 8715.3C safety standards. Users input telemetry parameters (O2 pressure, cabin temperature, mission elapsed time, gravity, alert flags) and receive an instant risk prediction with confidence score, alongside a live 3D WebGL flame visualization powered by real thermodynamic physics.

How the physics engine works:

The FastAPI backend computes genuine aerospace combustion physics — not approximations. It applies the First Law of Thermodynamics to calculate adiabatic flame temperature, Burke-Schumann diffusion theory for flame morphology, the Grashof number to model buoyancy effects (zero in microgravity), Fick's Law for molecular diffusion in 0G, and Wien's Displacement Law for spectral emission color. The result is a 3D flame that physically changes shape: a perfect sphere in microgravity (Aspect Ratio = 1.00) and an elongated plume in Earth gravity — matching what NASA actually observed aboard Apollo 13.

Benefits and intended impact:

The project demonstrates how AI and physics-based modeling can be combined to build predictive safety systems for high-risk aerospace environments. It makes complex fire risk assessment intuitive and visual — a concept directly applicable to spacecraft cabin safety monitoring, where early fire detection can be mission-critical. It also serves as an educational tool for understanding thermodynamics, machine learning classification, and NASA safety standards in an interactive, accessible format.

Tools, languages, and technologies used:

  • Python 3.12 — backend logic and ML pipeline
  • FastAPI + Uvicorn — REST API serving predictions in real-time
  • XGBoost — gradient-boosted decision tree classifier (~95% accuracy, 14 features)
  • Scikit-learn + Pandas + NumPy — data preprocessing and feature engineering
  • Three.js (WebGL) — 3D real-time flame rendering in the browser
  • Plotly.js — interactive telemetry charts with MET time replay
  • HTML5 / CSS3 / Vanilla JavaScript — frontend SPA with hash-based routing
  • Docker — containerization for cloud deployment
  • GitHub — version control and CI/CD integration
  • NASA Datasets — MSC-02680 telemetry, NPR 8715.3C, NASA-STD-8719.13, NASA SP-8067

Creativity and innovation:

Most fire risk tools display static charts or simple thresholds. Orbit-Deck goes further by coupling an AI prediction model directly with a physics simulation engine — the flame you see on screen is not decorative; it is computed from the same thermodynamic equations used in aerospace combustion research. The dashboard adopts a glass-cockpit design philosophy (caution and warning hierarchy, mission clock, subsystem tiles) inspired by real spacecraft primary display systems. The microgravity spherical flame behavior — a phenomenon unique to spaceflight — is rendered accurately in real-time WebGL, making an abstract physics concept visually tangible.

Factors considered:

  • Scientific accuracy — all thermodynamic formulas are grounded in published NASA standards and peer-reviewed combustion research
  • Safety standards compliance — risk matrix structure follows NPR 8715.3C and NASA-STD-8719.13
  • Accessibility — 100% English interface, keyboard navigation shortcuts (Alt+1 through Alt+7), ARIA labels, color never used as the sole risk indicator
  • Deployability — stateless API design, Dockerfile and Procfile included for one-command cloud deployment
  • Scalability — the prediction API accepts any telemetry payload; the model can be retrained on new datasets without changing the frontend
